doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
title: The entertainment tax on clubs
summary: The wartime cabaret tax applied to singing and hurt clubs that wanted both jazz and singers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: If there was singing they didn’t have to pay?

Did, yes. So they finally got the Congress to cut it five percent off, then they took another five percent off. And I don’t know if they ever completely eliminated it or if you still have to pay a percentage, but that was also a deterrent. Because you couldn’t — if the guy wanted to have jazz and the singers, so he could get both crowds, then that tax would kill him. So I hope I’ve answered your question.
